name: Kingdom of Iraq (British influence)
overview: The atlas labels one 1938 to 1945 polygon “Mesopotamia (GB),” but Iraq was an independent kingdom, not a British colony, throughout those map years. Its mandate ended with League of Nations admission in 1932. The 1930 Anglo-Iraqi treaty nevertheless preserved British bases, transit rights, and diplomatic influence. King Ghazi ruled until 1939; his young son Faisal II then inherited the crown under Regent Abd al-Ilah. Iraqi ministers, soldiers, officials, and nationalists argued over the alliance and the country’s future. In 1941 Rashid Ali and allied officers seized power, British and Empire forces fought their way back, and Baghdad’s Jews suffered the deadly Farhud. War strained prices, food, clothing, travel, and household budgets. Oil from Kirkuk, Basra’s date gardens, railways, airports, schools, medicine, radio, cinemas, religious communities, and women’s organizations show a society far larger than military diplomacy. Urban and rural life differed greatly, as did the opportunities of women, children, and minority communities. The atlas switches to an iraq id in 1945, but that is an editorial seam. The monarchy, treaty dispute, families, languages, farms, and towns continued.

periods.title: 1938 to 1939: An independent kingdom under an unequal alliance
periods.summary: The atlas begins this label in 1938, six years after Iraq’s League admission ended the British mandate. King Ghazi, parliament, ministers, and Iraqi officials governed, while the 1930 treaty preserved British air bases and transit rights. The label therefore needs a sovereignty warning, not a colonial flag of ownership.

periods.title: 1939 to 1940: Regency and European war
periods.summary: King Ghazi died in April 1939; his young son Faisal II inherited the crown, and Abd al-Ilah became regent. Britain entered war with Germany later that year. Iraqi political factions disputed whether treaty obligations, Arab nationalism, and anti-imperial independence could coexist. Railway and air networks became strategic resources.

periods.title: 1940 to 1941: Nationalist tension rises
periods.summary: Contemporary diplomacy reported fierce resentment of British influence despite formal independence. British treaty claims reached into ports, railways, river traffic, airfields, and communications. Baghdad radio and newspapers amplified political argument. The 1940 completion of rail connections toward Turkey made Iraq more connected and strategically exposed as regional war approached.

periods.title: 1941 to 1942: Coup, war, occupation, and Farhud
periods.summary: Rashid Ali and allied officers displaced the regent in April 1941. Iraqi forces besieged Habbaniya; British and Empire forces fought through May and restored the regency. The anti-Jewish Farhud in Baghdad on 1 and 2 June killed civilians and devastated homes and shops. Military victory did not settle legitimacy.

periods.title: 1942 to 1943: Wartime transit and fragile livelihoods
periods.summary: After the 1941 fighting, British influence remained powerful under the treaty and military presence. Iraq’s railways, ports, and airfields served Allied movement. Ordinary households faced the economic strain of war, while landowners, workers, civil servants, and traders experienced shortages differently. Government institutions continued to act under the regent and ministers.

periods.title: 1943 to 1944: Alliance and rationing
periods.summary: Iraq declared war on Axis powers in January 1943. Late that year officials prepared price controls and rationing, with tea, coffee, and sugar rationed from January 1944. These policies reached kitchens and markets unevenly. Iraqi archaeologists and state institutions also continued projects amid the wartime economy.

periods.title: 1944 to 1945: Reform pressure and atlas handoff
periods.summary: By 1945, Iraqi officials and diplomats openly discussed revising the 1930 treaty, which continued to privilege Britain. Women’s organizations were growing, and Iraq joined the Arab League. The atlas replaced mesopotamia-gb with iraq at 1945; that map seam marks neither new independence nor the creation of a republic.

sections.title: Read the label, territory, and sovereignty carefully

items.text: The imported name Mesopotamia (GB) is an atlas label, not the constitutional name of a British colony in 1938. Its generic summary misses the independent Iraqi monarchy. The id also lacked a reviewed card or override. This card keeps the exact identifier while naming the Kingdom of Iraq and its unequal British alliance.

The sole exact feature is a single polygon with one ring and 137 decoded positions. Its bounding box runs from about 34.98 to 48.55 degrees east and 28.42 to 37.33 degrees north. Baghdad, Basra, and Mosul test inside; Kuwait City and Damascus test outside. These are atlas measurements, not surveyed borders.

The exact id is absent from all other 49 audited snapshots. In 1930 sampled Iraqi cities sat beneath a broad United Kingdom layer; in 1945 they move to iraq and remain there in 1960. Neither repaint dates independence: Iraq left the mandate in 1932, and its monarchy survived 1945.

Iraq’s League of Nations admission in 1932 ended its mandate status. Contemporary diplomatic guarantees and judicial arrangements show that international recognition came with inherited obligations. Independence was legally real; it did not erase British bases, treaty rights, diplomatic pressure, or Iraqi arguments about how free the new state actually was.

The 1930 Anglo-Iraqi treaty provided the framework for British military facilities and transit. Iraqi ministers and soldiers still held their own offices and authority. Calling the kingdom simply British territory would erase that agency; calling it fully free of imperial power would erase the treaty’s privileged British position.

sections.title: Follow crown, parliament, administration, and nationalism

items.text: King Ghazi reigned as Iraq’s second Hashemite monarch until his fatal 1939 car accident. Constitutional ministries, parliament, and rival politicians operated around the palace. The dynasty was Iraqi state leadership, although British advisers and diplomats retained unusual access. Palace changes mattered, but they never spoke for every rural or urban household.

Faisal II inherited the throne as a child, so Abd al-Ilah served as regent. Prime ministers and cabinets shifted amid military pressure and conflict over the British alliance. A child king’s portrait could appear on public symbols while adults fought over policy; royal imagery must not be mistaken for unanimous consent.

Government reached people through ministries, courts, police, provincial officials, taxation, and schools, but its reach was uneven. Sunni Arab former Ottoman networks held many leading posts; Shi‘i Arabs, Kurds, Turkmens, Jews, Christians, and others lived under differing opportunities and pressures. No single official archive can capture all their political priorities.

Iraqi nationalism did not have one program. Some activists emphasized an independent Iraqi state and social reform; others imagined wider Arab unity. Kurdish claims, Shi‘i religious politics, class, and local loyalties complicated both. Debate over Britain’s bases could unite opponents temporarily without making their goals identical.

A US diplomat reported that treaty arrangements remained unpopular after League admission and that politicians used anti-British feeling in their contests. This is a contemporary outside assessment, not a poll of Iraqi opinion. The dissent helps explain 1941, while the report’s diplomatic viewpoint needs to stay visible.

sections.title: Confront the 1941 coup, war, coercion, and Farhud

items.text: Rashid Ali al-Gaylani and allied officers took control in April while the regent fled Baghdad. Britain refused to recognize the new cabinet. Iraqi actors sought greater autonomy but held different views of Axis support, Arab nationalism, and constitutional legitimacy. A coup is a struggle within Iraq as well as a confrontation with Britain.

Iraqi forces surrounded RAF Habbaniya; British aircraft attacked Iraqi positions from 2 May, and troops advanced across Iraq. Soldiers and civilians faced shelling, bombing, disrupted travel, and fear. The fighting restored a British-backed regency, but military success did not make the unequal alliance popular or morally simple.

British officials invoked treaty provisions for access to Iraq’s railways, rivers, ports, aerodromes, and communications. One 1941 letter even described proposed US use of a site as a British sublet requiring only notice to Iraqi authorities. The wording exposes how formal Iraqi sovereignty could coexist with deeply unequal wartime control.

On 1 and 2 June, anti-Jewish rioters killed and injured Baghdad civilians, assaulted women, and looted homes and shops in the Farhud. Some Iraqi neighbors sheltered Jewish families; soldiers and police were among perpetrators. Record estimates differ, so the human harm should be clear without pretending to one undisputed total.

Axis propaganda and the exiled Palestinian leader Hajj Amin al-Husayni influenced wartime politics, but evidence does not establish that his words directly caused the Farhud. British and Iraqi political choices, local antisemitism, and the violent transition of power mattered too. Accountability should follow documented actions, not a convenient single-villain story.

sections.title: Trace oil, date gardens, labor, and unequal wealth

items.text: The Iraq Petroleum Company’s concessions followed the 1927 discovery near Kirkuk and organized extraction for export. Oil created government revenue, engineering jobs, and international bargaining, but the consortium held powerful contractual rights. A pipeline can move crude across borders more easily than income reaches every farmer or neighborhood.

Kirkuk oil traveled toward Mediterranean outlets at Haifa and Tripoli on pipelines opened in the 1930s. Pump stations, crews, tankers, and overseas customers linked Iraqi land to a regional network. Wartime strategy heightened the system’s value; its route did not make all lands it crossed an Iraqi possession.

Concessions were negotiated by companies and Iraqi officials, not handed down by geography. Wartime diplomatic papers record talks over the Iraq Petroleum Company’s Basra rights. This was a continuing struggle over revenue and control, while major southern field development largely lay after the card’s interval. Avoid projecting later oil wealth backward.

Before southern oil expansion, Basra’s date palm gardens were a vital export landscape. Tenants, landholders, hired workers, merchants, and family members cultivated, packed, traded, and consumed dates along the Shatt al-Arab. The household economy was more varied than a single picture of either subsistence peasants or rich oilmen.

Land policy strengthened selected sheikhs and landlords while many cultivators remained dependent on shares, rents, and debts. The pattern varied by district and crop. Wartime demand and prices could reward owners differently from field workers, making economic growth an incomplete measure of ordinary security.

sections.title: Travel by rail, road, air, and sound

items.text: Iraqi State Railways’ 1939 and 1940 reports describe accounts, staff, engineering, rolling stock, and a northern connection through Mosul toward Syria and Turkey. The Baiji link was completed in 1940. Trains carried people, goods, and wartime demands, but a timetable did not make every village a station.

Baghdad and Basra civil airports had been developed during the 1930s, and Iraqi ministries issued notices to airmen. Air travel linked select cities and international routes; fares and airfields made it very different from ordinary walking, carts, riverboats, or trains. An airport marks technical capacity, not universal mobility.

Baghdad broadcasts reached listeners in Arabic, English, German, and Italian during the 1941 crisis. Monitors preserved claims made amid fighting, but broadcasts were political acts, and English transcriptions may omit tone or distort words. A radio could connect distant audiences quickly while also carrying rumor and wartime propaganda.

A 1940 military route report measured roads from Baghdad through Kirkuk toward Iran and recorded water, fuel, railways, and camps. It was compiled for strategic movement, so its detail says more about military priorities than whether ordinary families could afford travel. Roads connected some places while leaving others arduous to reach.

Cinema owners brought Egyptian, Indian, and Hollywood films into Baghdad and provincial towns. Iraqi Jewish entrepreneurs were active in distribution alongside other businesspeople. Screens, tickets, posters, and shared laughter show urban leisure beyond palace politics, although audience records cannot represent every class, village, or generation.

sections.title: Work the countryside and feed households

items.text: Irrigation along the Tigris and Euphrates supported grain, rice, vegetables, and date palms, while floods, drought, drainage, and land rights shaped yields. A 1952 official survey helps describe inherited systems, but its later observations cannot be pasted unchanged onto every 1938 farm. Water management joined engineering to labor and bargaining.

Rural families planted, harvested, tended animals, carried water, cooked, repaired shelter, and negotiated access to fields. Sharecropping and landholding arrangements differed across Iraq. Government descriptions often treated a male landholder as the entire household, hiding women’s and children’s labor that made cultivation possible.

Studies of the Lower Euphrates describe rural women’s farm work, animal care, food preparation, and difficult access to schooling and medicine under the monarchy. This is one regional history, not a portrait of every Iraqi woman. Wealth, town or village, religion, family, and season changed what daily work required.

A British political review says high prices for meat, fruit, and vegetables strained poorer urban residents. Rationing of tea, coffee, and sugar began in January 1944, followed by some textiles. The report describes policy and hardship, but households still traded, substituted, borrowed, grew, or went without in different ways.

The Dujayla land settlement began as a pilot in 1945, aiming to place some landless families on newly irrigated state land. Such projects exposed the monarchy’s recognition of rural inequality, yet canals and plots alone could not repair every debt, gender hierarchy, or relationship with powerful landlords. Its outcomes belong beyond this map seam.

sections.title: Enter neighborhoods, homes, and plural social worlds

items.text: Baghdad, Basra, Mosul, Kirkuk, holy cities, market towns, and villages held different mixes of languages, livelihoods, faiths, and built spaces. Sunni and Shi‘i Muslims, Jews, Christians, Kurds, Turkmens, and others were not a single social type. The atlas polygon can include places without explaining what any particular street felt like.

Baghdad’s Jewish community had schools, merchants, craftsmen, families, and religious institutions. Jewish children’s schooling developed within communal and state settings, with language and curriculum choices reflecting wider Iraqi society. The Farhud later damaged trust and safety, but it must not reduce an old, complex community to a single episode of victimhood.

The Iraqi Bahai community organized a national spiritual assembly in 1931 and maintained religious and property affairs through the monarchy. Its experience shows both public participation and vulnerability to legal and religious opposition. Baghdad’s social map included such minority networks even when the atlas painted everyone with one political color.

Clothes, tea, coffee, sugar, meat, fruit, and vegetables became subjects of price or ration decisions during wartime. A shop queue was part of political economy, yet families with land, wages, remittances, or merchant contacts faced very different choices. The records do not establish one universal meal or wardrobe for 1944.

Cinema businesses linked shopkeepers, projectionists, importers, audiences, and relatives across Baghdad and smaller towns. Movies could offer amusement and news of distant places, but commercial records mostly preserve owners and transactions. They reveal less about who took a child along, who stayed home, or how a family discussed the story afterward.

sections.title: Hear women, children, schools, and languages

items.text: Educated Iraqi women wrote poems, studied medicine and law, joined clubs, and helped political campaigns. Some supported resistance to Britain in 1941. These visible women were often urban and comparatively privileged; their work does not cancel the farm, domestic, market, and care labor of women whose names rarely reached print.

The Iraqi Women’s Union was founded in 1945 amid a wider field of women’s associations. Later accounts disagree about the balance of nationalist, charitable, reformist, and leftist work. The organization is an achievement in public action, but one elite union cannot stand for every woman’s politics or legal position.

Girls’ secondary education expanded in the 1930s, but access clustered among city families. Boys and girls could encounter different curricula; religious communities also supported their own schools. Children outside classrooms still learned farm, trade, language, and household skills. School growth was meaningful without implying universal attendance or one Iraqi childhood.

Baghdad’s Jewish schools illustrate how learning could pass through community institutions as well as state classrooms. Families weighed languages, faith, qualifications, and livelihoods. Their experience complicates any claim that one ministry controlled all education. It also reminds us that a child’s day involved friends, chores, streets, and home beyond lesson books.

Hashim al-Witri and Muammar Khalid al-Shabandar’s 1939 Baghdad book bears «تاريخ الطب في العراق مع نشوء وتقدم الكلية الطبية الملكية العراقية» (Tārīkh al-ṭibb fī al-ʿIrāq maʿa nushūʾ wa-taqaddum al-kulliyya al-ṭibbiyya al-malakiyya al-ʿirāqiyya), meaning “History of medicine in Iraq, with the establishment and development of the Royal Iraqi Medical College.” It cannot represent all Iraqi languages or everyday speech.

sections.title: Meet doctors, patients, and public health limits

items.text: Baghdad’s Royal College of Medicine trained Iraqi doctors alongside longer networks of practitioners and nurses. Its graduates and faculty expanded local capacity, but a medical school did not place a physician near every village. Hospitals, families, midwives, and traditional healers remained part of the care people could actually reach.

A 1939 Arabic history of medicine and the Iraqi medical college is itself evidence of Iraqi professional writing. It documents local interest in training and institutions, though a digitized book catalog cannot prove how many patients received treatment. Medical achievements belong to Iraqi workers as well as foreign advisers.

A University of Baghdad study of the 1930s identifies malaria and bilharzia among major disease burdens and describes weak public health resources. Such illness connected irrigation, housing, work, and access to treatment. Numbers and causes varied by locality; national health language should not flatten a child in Mosul and a farmer near Basra into one case.

A contemporary medical history looked at health services and training near this interval. It reveals institutional ambition but cannot certify a specific 1940 household’s access. Contemporary disease scholarship likewise shows infections enduring while distance, income, and uneven sanitation constrained care. Training more doctors mattered without making rural medicine suddenly equal.

Care began at home: relatives watched fever, found food and clean water, sought medicines, or arranged transport. Rural women’s histories show how such labor fitted among cultivation, animals, and children. Formal health reports usually measure clinics and doctors more readily than a long night beside a sick family member.

sections.title: Carry water, manage waste, and notice enduring work

items.text: River and canal water sustained fields and towns, while safe drinking water required separate collection, treatment, carrying, and storage. A later land-development study discusses irrigation ambitions but cannot supply a 1940 tap count. The water story includes engineering and the repeated daily work of people who lifted and guarded it.

Iraq’s national library catalogs a Baghdad Water Committee administrative report dated 1945. That establishes an active municipal water institution, not universal connection or purity in every house. The record is bibliographic rather than the report’s full text, so this card draws no numerical household coverage claim from it.

Earlier Basra administration records discuss public latrines, private cesspits, waste collection, and water delivery. They prove that sanitation demanded facilities and workers before this interval, but cannot be reused as a 1940 inventory. Toilets had to be built, cleaned, and reached; no atlas polygon supplies that missing household count.

No source here establishes that all Iraqi homes had flush toilets, private latrines, or sewer connections in 1938 to 1945. Earlier descriptions instead show why disposal, water, maintenance, and access must be separated. A toilet is modest engineering with an immodest job; its history deserves honest evidence.

Iraqi government excavations at Aqar Quf continued in 1942 to 1944 and entered scholarly publication during wartime. Together with rail operations, medical training, and women’s organizing, this was part of living Iraqi work and achievement. Ancient Mesopotamian sites matter, but they should not replace the twentieth-century people on this card.

ending.text: At the atlas’s 1945 boundary, the exact mesopotamia-gb id vanishes and sampled Iraqi cities move to an iraq feature. The map change did not create Iraqi independence: the British mandate ended in 1932. It did not make Iraq a republic either; the Hashemite monarchy continued until 1958. In 1945 Iraqi officials sought revision of the 1930 alliance, demonstrating that British privileges endured beyond this card’s range. Iraq was a founding United Nations member and ratified the Charter on 21 December 1945. The next atlas label therefore represents editorial continuity of the Iraqi state, not a clean break in sovereignty, society, or culture. Families, farms, cities, schools, faith communities, women’s associations, and political disagreement all crossed this cartographic seam. British influence and Iraqi resistance to it also persisted.
